 Follow Why are pools and youth programs part of Toledo's Issue 16? Here's what could be cut if the levy fails
 Faith Zochowski Tue, November 3, 2026 at 4:13 AM UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Faith Zochowski/WTOL 11 Toledo voters will head to the polls Tuesday to decide whether to approve Issue 16, a proposed quarter-percent increase to the city's income tax aimed at funding public safety initiatives. City leaders say the levy would generate about $25 million annually over the next four years and could help avoid cuts to police and fire services.
 "If you don't have a safe city, I don't know how you'd be a great city," Toledo City Councilman George Sarantou said.
 According to city leaders, levy funds would be restricted to public safety efforts, including expanding police and fire recruit classes, supporting gang enforcement initiatives and increasing residential traffic enforcement.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement During the Oct. 28 Toledo City Council Finance Committee meeting, Deputy Mayor Abby Arnold said the city's current budget projections include 73 layoffs if additional revenue is not secured. City administration officials say roughly half of those potential layoffs would come from police and fire.
 Those concerns are shared by Toledo firefighters.
 Toledo Firefighters Local 92 President Joe Cira says the department is already operating under staffing pressures.
 He says the department currently has no spare engines or medic units available, one ambulance in west Toledo has been out of service since last week, and crews recently operated 10 firefighters below minimum staffing levels over the weekend.
 Advertisement Advertisement The city's list of potential cuts extends beyond police and fire.
 Officials have also identified youth programs, city pools and other services as areas that could face reductions if additional funding is not approved.
 When asked why pools and youth programs are being discussed as part of a public safety conversation, Sarantou said those services help keep young people engaged during the summer months.
 " If we don't have youth programs available… then we really have kids with a lot of time on their hands," Sarantou said.
 Sarantou also argues years of reduced state funding have contributed to Toledo's financial challenges. He said the city has lost $288 million each year over the past 18 years, and believes those reductions have caught up with municipalities across Ohio.
 Advertisement Advertisement "People are asking, why is this such a problem now? Well, it's because our state has let us down for 18 years and it's caught up with us," he said.
 Still, not everyone is convinced a tax increase is the answer.
 Some voters told WTOL 11 they support the levy because they believe additional funding could improve staffing levels and public safety response times.
 "If it's keeping our community safe and us safe ... I would not have a problem at all. Take that out of my check, please do," voter Taure Williams said.
 Others remain opposed.
 "I pay enough taxes. No more taxes," voter Wendy Owens said.
 City leaders stress that the cuts discussed so far are only potential scenarios and that no final decisions have been made. Any changes to the city's budget would ultimately require action by Toledo City Council after the election.
 Advertisement Advertisement Sarantou also acknowledged that even if Issue 16 passes, Toledo is still projected to face a budget deficit in the coming years, meaning officials will likely continue searching for ways to reduce spending.
